title: Documentation
intro: Connect your coding assistant to Overpass verified routes, and call the provider simulator from your tests.

start.intro: Three steps, nothing to install: the Overpass MCP server is already running, and your editor connects to it over HTTP.

token.title: Create an MCP token
token.text: In settings, Tokens tab, create a token for the “MCP server” usage. It is shown only once.

config.title: Copy the configuration
config.text: Paste your editor's configuration, token included. Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code are covered below.

ask.title: Ask your question
ask.text: Ask your assistant to integrate a service: it finds the route, reads its state and writes the code from it.

editors.intro: The configurations below hold a placeholder token. Once you create a token, settings show the same configurations with your real token.
editors.readOnly: The server is read-only and embeds no AI model: your assistant brings its own. It reads Overpass only through the API, with your token; a revoked token is refused on the very next call.

tools.caption: The four MCP server tools
tools.name: Tool

search_routes.output: Routes with their state and last check date

get_route.output: Route content, state, last check, potholes

list_potholes.input: route identifier, or service and country

list_services.output: Covered services and countries, simulator availability

tools.safety: Route content is written by members. The server returns it inside an <overpass_data> block, preceded by a notice: this is data, not instructions. Every answer repeats the route's state and last check date, so your assistant warns you when it is old or reported broken.

example.intro: An end-to-end example, with a fictional route. The tool calls are made by your assistant itself: you only write the question.
example.question: Write the Laravel controller that receives the Wave Checkout webhook in Côte d'Ivoire and verifies its signature.
example.searchTitle: 2. The assistant searches for a route
example.readTitle: 3. It reads the route, its state and its potholes

example.codeTitle: 4. It writes the code from the route
example.code:
<?php
// Based on Overpass route 3f2b8c1e (state clear, checked on 14 October 2026).
// Pothole confirmed on the route: Wave may send the same webhook twice.

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;

class WaveWebhookController extends Controller
{
    public function __invoke(Request $request)
    {
        parse_str(str_replace(',', '&', (string) $request->header('Wave-Signature')), $sig);
        $payload = ($sig['t'] ?? '') . $request->getContent();
        $expected = hash_hmac('sha256', $payload, config('services.wave.webhook_secret'));
        abort_unless(hash_equals($expected, $sig['v1'] ?? ''), 401);

        $event = $request->json()->all();
        // Each event is handled once, even when it arrives twice.
        if (! Cache::add('wave-event:' . $event['id'], true, now()->addDay())) {
            return response()->noContent();
        }

        // Mark the order as paid here.
        return response()->noContent();
    }
}
example.warning: Had the route been reported broken, never checked, or last checked more than 90 days ago, the assistant would have said so before offering this code.
